clinicalPearls: Mildest phenotype of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum, usually caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function NLRP3 variants; a clinically similar NLRP12-associated form (sometimes termed FCAS2) is also recognised.
Attacks follow generalised environmental cold exposure rather than direct local contact, typically after a delay of an hour or two, and are often reproducible.
Episodes are brief, commonly settling within a day, and comprise a cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fever, chills, arthralgia, conjunctivitis and headache.
Unlike acquired cold contact urticaria, the local ice-cube provocation test is negative because it is systemic cooling, not local contact, that provokes symptoms.
Symptoms tend to be worse in the evening and can be triggered by air-conditioned or refrigerated environments as well as outdoor cold.
Sensorineural hearing loss and amyloidosis are uncommon at this mild end but overlap with Muckle-Wells syndrome can occur, so surveillance remains prudent.
Interleukin-1 blockade is highly effective for troublesome disease, alongside practical avoidance of cold exposure.
Acute-phase reactants rise during a cold-provoked attack and can help confirm a systemic inflammatory response.
reference.pathophysiology: Gain-of-function NLRP3 variants lower the activation threshold of the cryopyrin inflammasome, which in this phenotype is triggered by a fall in temperature. Cold-induced assembly of the inflammasome activates caspase-1, driving maturation and release of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 and producing a self-limiting burst of neutrophil-rich systemic inflammation. Because the underlying molecular lesion is shared with the more severe cryopyrin-associated syndromes, the mechanism and treatment response mirror those conditions, differing chiefly in the milder degree of constitutive activation and the requirement for a cold stimulus.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary recurrent fevers such as familial Mediterranean fever
additionalInvestigations: NLRP3 gene analysis, with NLRP12 testing where the phenotype fits but NLRP3 is negative
Generalised (evaporative) cold provocation with monitoring of symptoms and inflammatory markers
Local ice-cube contact test to distinguish from acquired cold urticaria
Acute-phase reactants measured before and after cold challenge
Skin biopsy showing a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis
Baseline audiometry to detect any overlap with Muckle-Wells syndrome
redFlags: Emerging sensorineural hearing loss suggesting progression towards a more severe cryopyrin-associated phenotype
Proteinuria raising the possibility of AA amyloidosis
Neurological features such as chronic headache or papilloedema that are atypical for the mild phenotype
Persistently raised inflammatory markers between cold-provoked attacks
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable, with cold avoidance and interleukin-1 blockade providing effective control and a low risk of the amyloidosis seen at the severe end of the spectrum. Quality of life can nonetheless be significantly affected in cold climates without treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with acquired cold contact urticaria and being misled by a negative local ice-cube test
Expecting immediate rather than delayed symptom onset after cold exposure
Assuming a negative NLRP3 result excludes the diagnosis without considering NLRP12-associated disease
Neglecting audiological and renal surveillance because the phenotype appears mild
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice (current edition)
SHARE recommendations for the management of autoinflammatory diseases
Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology (current edition)
management: Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra, canakinumab or rilonacept as the disease-specific therapy for frequent or severe attacks
Avoidance of generalised cold exposure, including air-conditioned and refrigerated environments, as the first-line preventive measure
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptomatic relief of arthralgia and fever during milder attacks
Surveillance for AA amyloidosis with periodic urinalysis for proteinuria and renal monitoring
Baseline and periodic audiometry to detect sensorineural hearing loss overlapping with Muckle-Wells syndrome
Genetic counselling with NLRP3, or NLRP12, testing and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
Specialist immunology or rheumatology follow-up to track inflammatory markers and escalate to interleukin-1 blockade if amyloidosis risk emerges
